regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 55.9","signal_text":"India GDP at 7.8% YoY looks unimpeachable until you note the RBI's own forecast sits at 6.7% YoY — a 110bps gap that historically reflects deflator assumptions, not real output gains. PMI Composite at 55.9 and IIP at 8.0% YoY corroborate momentum, but core sector at 4.8% YoY (decelerating from 5.0%) and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity suggest the expansion is real but narrowing. The quality question: services PMI at 55.2 is doing the heavy lifting; manufacturing at 55.1 is solid but not accelerating.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 5.54% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY — a 95th-percentile print, up 288bps in a single month — is the number the RBI cannot dismiss as noise. Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY is already above the 4% target midpoint, but core CPI at 3.9% YoY tells a different story: the pressure is supply-side, not demand-driven. The trap is that Brent has fallen from $113/bbl to $97.89/bbl over three months, yet fuel inflation is still accelerating — which means the pass-through mechanism is lagged and the relief, when it comes, will also lag.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.4% YoY; CD ratio 81%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.4% YoY against deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160bps divergence widening for two consecutive months — keeps the CD ratio at 81%, the 73rd percentile historically. The last time India sustained a CD ratio above 80% during a rate-pause cycle was FY14; within 12 months, external shock forced an emergency reversal. NBFC credit accelerating to 15.8% YoY (from 10.0%) adds a second layer: NBFCs fund at the margin, and margin funding dries up fastest when sentiment turns.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is unchanged, but the RBI's own inflation forecast has moved to 5.1% YoY — leaving a real rate of roughly 14bps, barely positive. That is insufficient buffer if fuel pass-through continues into December CPI. The incentive structure is clear: cut too early and imported inflation feeds back through a weaker INR; hold too long and credit costs choke the capex cycle that capacity utilisation at 77.4% is just beginning to justify.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (up from 16.1%) and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity — a three-year high — are the two most credible signals that private investment is genuinely underway, not just budgeted. The inversion: capacity utilisation crosses 80% before private capex commitments typically accelerate; at 77.4%, India is close but not there. Core sector at 4.8% YoY, decelerating from 5.0%, is the one discordant note — cement and steel dispatch are the honest proxies, and they are not yet confirming the IIP headline.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹203521 cr/mo; PV 7.9% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,03,521 cr / month is a record, but the composition matters: the prior month was ₹1,99,853 cr / month, suggesting genuine sequential momentum rather than a base-effect spike. Passenger vehicle sales at 7.9% YoY are decelerating sharply (from 26.1% three months ago), while two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY are surging — the classic India dual-economy signal where mass-market rural demand is recovering faster than urban discretionary. Commercial vehicle sales at 12.6% YoY, falling for two consecutive months, suggest freight operators are not yet convinced the cycle is durable.","badge_label":"Stable Consumption","badge_type":"b-neu"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.4% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160 bps divergence widening for 2 consecutive months (17.1%→19.4% credit; 9.9%→17.8% deposits). CD ratio at 81% credit ÷ deposits, down from 82.2% but still at 73rd percentile historically. NBFC credit accelerating at 15.8% YoY (up from 10% YoY), now at 57th percentile. Services credit surging at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile), agriculture at 17.2% YoY (78th percentile).","implication":"The deposit acceleration masks a structural problem: credit is outpacing deposits by 160 bps, forcing banks to rely on costlier wholesale funding and NBFCs to tap bond markets. Overweight private banks with CASA ratios > 45% and deposit franchises in metros — they'll poach deposits from smaller lenders. Underweight NBFCs with wholesale funding > 30% of liabilities; their cost of funds will compress margins. Watch for RBI to signal deposit-friendly measures (higher savings rates, CRR cuts) within 2-3 months if this gap persists.","pct_10y":73,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 73rd percentile is elevated but not crisis-level; however, the 160 bps credit-deposit gap is the widest in 18 months. Last time this divergence was this acute (2022), RBI tightened liquidity and smaller banks faced deposit flight.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Cycle Firing on All Cylinders","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (latest, up from 16.1% YoY), at 52nd percentile. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (up from 75.6%), at 74th percentile — highest in 3 years. Core sector growth at 4.8% YoY (50th percentile), a modest deceleration from 5% but still positive. Credit to industry at 18.2% YoY (74th percentile), services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile). PMI manufacturing at 55.1 index (75th percentile), services at 55.2 index (84th percentile).","implication":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% signals capex will accelerate further — firms are bumping against constraints and will invest to expand. Overweight capital goods, cement, and steel stocks; underweight consumer discretionary. Allocate to infrastructure-linked debt (PSU bonds, infrastructure NBFCs). The services credit surge (24.3% YoY) suggests IT capex and GCC expansion — watch for office absorption data to confirm (latest: 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter, down sharply from 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter prior, a red flag for IT capex momentum).","pct_10y":74,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 77.4% is at the 74th percentile and typically precedes 12-18 months of sustained capex. The last time CU was this high (2018-2019), capex growth averaged 18% YoY.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Inflows Hit Record, But Growth Stalling","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (latest), at 93rd percentile — rising 3 consecutive months (₹29,845 cr → ₹31,961 cr → ₹32,297 cr → ₹32,490 cr). SIP accounts at 10.0646 mn (latest), at 2nd percentile (data quality issue: prior reading was 9.9 mn, suggesting a data anomaly). SIP AUM at ₹17.86 lakh cr (89th percentile), up 2 of last 3 months. However, SIP YoY growth at 10.7% (30th percentile), decelerating from 15% YoY three months ago. Equity MF net inflows at ₹38,307 cr / month (80th percentile), up from ₹29,329 cr / month.","implication":"SIP inflows are at record nominal levels but growth is decelerating sharply (15% → 10.7% YoY) — a classic late-cycle signal. The divergence between rising inflows and slowing growth suggests affluent money entering (larger ticket sizes), not mass retail. Reduce equity MF exposure; rotate into debt MFs and fixed income. Monitor SIP account growth closely — if it turns negative, retail participation is waning. DII flows remain strong (₹51,829 cr / month net, 95th percentile), but FII flows are deeply negative (₹-49,935 cr / month net, 17th percentile), creating a structural bid-ask imbalance.","pct_10y":93,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 93rd percentile are historically associated with market peaks; the last time inflows were this high (2021), the Nifty corrected 20% within 6 months. Slowing YoY growth is the canary.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens RBI's Pause","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (latest, up from 20.05% YoY), at 95th percentile — a 288 bps jump in one month. WPI at 9.92% YoY (up from 9.78% YoY), at 67th percentile. Food inflation at 7.74% YoY (up from 5.97% YoY), at 57th percentile, rising 2 consecutive months. Brent crude at $97.89 / bbl (flat), WTI at $90.8 / bbl (flat), but both down from $113.4 / bbl and $104.1 / bbl respectively 3 months ago. Natural gas at $2.993 / MMBtu (18th percentile), stable. FAO food index at 136 index (61st percentile), up from 130.3 index.","implication":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY is a structural headwind that will keep headline CPI elevated (currently 5.54% YoY, above RBI's 4% target). RBI's rate pause is at risk if fuel inflation persists — expect hawkish commentary at the next MPC meeting. Hedge energy exposure; overweight oil & gas stocks and refiners (they benefit from high crude). Avoid consumer staples with high fuel-linked costs (logistics, FMCG). The FAO food index uptick suggests food inflation will remain sticky. Allocate to inflation-hedging assets (gold, commodities, TIPS-equivalent Indian instruments).","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is the highest in 3 years; the last time it spiked this high (2022), RBI hiked rates 190 bps over 6 months. Current pause is vulnerable.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"Fed Tightening Cycle Accelerating, Carry Unwind Risk","data_text":"Fed funds rate at 3.88% p.a. (up from 3.75% p.a.), at 69th percentile, rising 3 consecutive months (3.63% → 3.63% → 3.75% → 3.88%). US 10Y Treasury yield at 4.84% yield (down from 4.9%), at 87th percentile, but recent trend is down 1 of last 5 months (5% → 4.99% → 5.05% → 4.98% → 4.94% → 4.84%). BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (up from 1%), at 100th percentile, rising 2 consecutive months (0.75% → 1% → 1.25%). ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (up from 2.25%), at 63rd percentile. US PMI composite at 58.4 index (91st percentile), rising 2 consecutive months. US GDP at 3.4% SAAR (up from 2.2%), at 51st percentile.","implication":"The Fed is tightening (funds rate up 25 bps in one month) while the BOJ is normalizing (1.25% is the highest in 20 years), compressing the carry trade that has funded EM and India flows. FII outflows from India (₹-49,935 cr / month net) are a direct consequence. Reduce leverage; hedge INR exposure; avoid high-beta EM assets. The US 10Y yield at 4.84% (87th percentile) is a structural ceiling for Indian bond yields — expect 10Y GSec yields to stay elevated. Overweight USD-denominated assets and reduce INR-denominated equity exposure. Watch for further BOJ tightening — if it reaches 1.5% p.a., carry unwind will accelerate.","pct_10y":87,"pct_note":"US 10Y at 87th percentile and Fed funds rising is historically associated with EM capital flight; the last time this occurred (2018), India saw ₹1.5 lakh cr in FII outflows over 6 months.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Weakening Despite RBI Intervention Signals","data_text":"INR at ₹93.46 / USD (down from ₹93.89 / USD), at 85th percentile — but recent trend shows INR weakening 1 of last 5 months (₹97.09 → ₹96.15 → ₹95.24 → ₹94.34 → ₹95.24 → ₹94.34, latest ₹93.46 is a reversal). DXY at 102.217 index (56th percentile), flat. FII equity net flows at ₹-49,935 cr / month net (17th percentile), deeply negative. India VIX at 18.43 index (14th percentile), rising from 15.3 index 2 months ago. Gold in INR at ₹12,351 / g (100th percentile), at all-time highs.","implication":"INR weakness despite RBI's visible intervention (INR at 85th percentile suggests RBI is defending) indicates structural FII outflows are overwhelming RBI's capacity to support the currency. The ₹-49,935 cr / month FII outflow is the smoking gun — carry trade unwind and Fed tightening are driving capital out. Hedge INR exposure via forwards or options; reduce unhedged USD liabilities. Expect RBI to signal higher rates or intervention at the next policy meeting. Gold at all-time highs in INR is a risk-off signal — allocate to defensive assets. Monitor FII flows weekly; if they turn positive, INR will stabilize.","pct_10y":85,"pct_note":"INR at 85th percentile weakness with FII outflows is a 2018-2019 pattern; the last time FII flows were this negative, INR weakened 8% over 3 months before RBI tightened.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Collapse Signals IT Capex Stall","data_text":"Office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter (latest), down 79% from 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter prior quarter — a cliff-edge decline. Office vacancy at 13.4% vacant (down from 14.5%), at 36th percentile, suggesting supply-side normalization, not demand strength. Nifty IT index flat while Nifty 50 up 9% YoY — IT stocks are decoupling from the broader market. Services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile) is surging, but this is driven by non-IT services (hospitality, logistics, healthcare). Rent in Bengaluru at ₹103.6 / sqft / mo (down from ₹168.8 / sqft / mo), Mumbai at ₹156 / sqft / mo (down from ₹342.6 / sqft / mo) — both down 40%+ from peaks. Airline passenger traffic at 86.4 mn / month (35th percentile), flat.","implication":"The office absorption collapse is NOT a demand story — it's a GCC (Global Capability Center) consolidation story. Indian IT services firms are not expanding footprints; instead, multinational GCCs are consolidating into fewer, larger hubs (Bangalore, Hyderabad). This means: (1) IT services capex is stalling, contradicting the 'capex upcycle' narrative; (2) commercial real estate (Embassy, Mindspace, Brookfield REITs) are facing structural headwinds, not cyclical ones; (3) the services credit surge is NOT IT-driven, it's healthcare, logistics, and fintech. Underweight IT services stocks and commercial REITs. Overweight healthcare and logistics stocks instead. The office vacancy decline is a false positive — it's driven by supply constraints, not demand recovery. Falsifiable: if office absorption rebounds to > 12 mn sq ft / quarter in the next 2 quarters, this thesis is wrong.","pct_10y":0,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter is at the 0th percentile (lowest on record for this dataset), a structural break from the 14-19 mn sq ft / quarter range of prior quarters. This is the first time in the capex cycle that office demand has collapsed while credit growth accelerated — a divergence that signals sectoral rotation, not broad-based capex.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP, 4.8% Core Sector — The Headline Flatters

The facts:

  • India GDP at 7.8% YoY sits 110bps above the RBI's own forecast of 6.7% YoY — a gap that historically reflects deflator assumptions rather than real output.
  • PMI Composite at 55.9 and IIP at 8.0% YoY confirm expansion, but core sector at 4.8% YoY (decelerating from 5.0%) is the honest proxy for goods-economy momentum.
  • Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity — a three-year high — is approaching but not yet at the 80% threshold that historically triggers private capex commitments.
  • But two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY vs passenger vehicle sales at 7.9% YoY (falling two months in a row) signals rural recovery outpacing urban discretionary — a consumption mix that rarely sustains premium earnings.

The tension: The GDP headline and the PMI agree; the core sector and vehicle-sales mix do not. Growth is real but narrower than the 7.8% YoY print implies, concentrated in services and rural mass-market rather than broad-based industrial output.

Bottom line: Watch core sector YoY: a third consecutive deceleration below 4.5% YoY would signal the goods economy is diverging from the services-led headline.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US Acceleration Meets Rising Fear — The VIX Tells the Real Story

The facts:

  • US GDP at 3.4% SAAR (up from 2.2% SAAR) and US PMI Composite at 58.4 (91st percentile) signal the strongest US growth pulse in two years.
  • But US VIX at 25.64 — rising four months in a row from 17.52 — is pricing tail risk that the PMI survey is not.
  • S&P 500 at 7,377 (100th percentile) and Nasdaq at 24,579 are both falling five of the last five months — the index level flatters; the trend does not.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, rising two months in a row) is the underappreciated accelerant: yen carry unwind compresses EM risk appetite with a 4–6 week lag.

The tension: US growth data says re-acceleration; US equity trend and VIX say something is breaking under the surface. BOJ tightening into this environment is the second-order risk consensus has not priced — it drains global liquidity precisely when US credit spreads are widening.

Bottom line: If US VIX sustains above 25, expect FII equity outflows from India to accelerate beyond the current ₹49,935 cr / month run-rate.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

DII Absorption Holding — But SIP Growth Rate Is the Warning

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile) have risen three consecutive months, providing a structural floor under domestic equity demand.
  • But SIP YoY growth at 10.7% YoY (30th percentile) has decelerated from 15.0% YoY three months ago — the stock of inflows is high; the flow of new participants is slowing.
  • DII equity net inflows at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile) are absorbing FII outflows of ₹49,935 cr / month — a near-perfect offset that cannot be assumed to persist.
  • NFO collections at ₹998 cr / month (2nd percentile) confirm retail appetite for new product is near a decade low — existing SIPs are sticky; incremental mobilisation is not.

The tension: The liquidity picture looks balanced only because DII absorption is running at a 95th-percentile pace against FII selling. SIP growth deceleration means the DII buffer is not expanding — it is holding. Any further FII acceleration breaks the equilibrium.

Bottom line: Watch monthly SIP YoY growth: a print below 10.0% YoY would signal the retail liquidity floor is eroding faster than the headline inflow number suggests.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

Bank Nifty at 98th Percentile, Office REITs Down 30% — Two Markets, One Economy

The facts:

  • NRI residential buying is falling — NRI share at 18% of purchases (down 2pp), with NRI share within premium/luxury at 32%; remittances at $144.8 bn (16% YoY) are strong but not translating into property demand.
  • Hyderabad leads residential momentum: sales +15% YoY, launches +120% YoY, 28 months unsold inventory — a supply surge that will test pricing power within six quarters.
  • Bank Nifty at 58,851 (98th percentile) is pricing a credit cycle that the CD ratio at 81% and deposit growth deceleration should be discounting, not celebrating.
  • But Embassy REIT at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, and Brookfield at ₹263/unit are all down 11–31% from prior prints — office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter (a cliff from 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter prior) is the market the REIT prices are finally acknowledging.

The tension: Bank Nifty at a 10-year-high percentile and office REITs at multi-year lows are not contradictory — they are sequential. Banks fund the credit cycle; REITs price the IT capex stall that follows when the cycle turns. The equity market has not connected these dots yet.

Bottom line: Avoid office REITs until absorption recovers above 10 mn sq ft / quarter; hedge Bank Nifty longs against a macro-prudential risk-weight circular on unsecured lending.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Four Fuses, One Detonator — Sequence Matters

The facts:

  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) forces RBI to hold even as growth needs accommodation — the longer the pause, the sharper the eventual pivot and the more violent the bond market reaction.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile) unwinding yen carry — with US VIX at 25.64 and rising — is the global liquidity shock that arrives without a press conference.
  • FII equity outflows at ₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile) against a DII buffer that is not growing: one month of SIP deceleration below ₹30,000 cr / month removes the offset.
  • Hyderabad residential launches at +120% YoY against 28 months of unsold inventory — a supply overhang that reprices the premium segment and hits developer credit quality within 12–18 months.

The tension: Each risk is manageable in isolation; the danger is sequencing — BOJ triggers FII outflows, FII outflows stress the INR, INR weakness feeds fuel inflation, fuel inflation locks the RBI, and the RBI's paralysis is what finally breaks the credit cycle.

Bottom line: Watch US VIX this week: a sustained close above 27 would signal the BOJ carry-unwind is accelerating and India's FII outflow run-rate will worsen materially.

"}
